blocks.note: The whole file is plumbing. No AI call happens here, and nothing decides anything. It is 80 lines on purpose: you can read all of it before trusting it. Start it with "node bot.ts" from inside the passagens.ts folder, and stop it with Ctrl+C.

App is Slack's own class, from the @slack/bolt package. It handles the connection, the reconnects and the parsing of each event, and hands you one plain function per message. Everything else from that package stays unused.

The single door into the brain. responder is defined at the bottom of harness/agente.ts (around line 374 there) and takes a conversation id, your text and a progress callback. Nothing else in the graph is reachable from here, which is why the brain can be rewritten without touching this file.

ligarMonitor is defined in harness/monitor.ts (around line 82). It starts the clock that re-prices your watched routes, and it is the only thing in the project that makes the bot speak without being asked.

Node reads the .env file and copies each KEY=value line into process.env, which is what makes the next lines work. Watch the relative path: ".env" means the folder you ran the command from, so this line only works when you start the bot from inside passagens.ts. The other files use import.meta.dirname instead, which does not care where you are.

The Slack connection, and three settings worth knowing. token is the bot's own badge (xoxb-...), what it posts as. appToken (xapp-...) is the permission to open a socket from your Mac. socketMode: true is the one that matters most: your Mac dials out to Slack instead of Slack calling in, so you need no public address, no tunnel and no server. That single line is why this bot can run on a laptop.

A Map from a channel id to the promise of whatever is currently running in that channel. It exists because the conversation memory for a channel is one saved record (harness/agente.ts sets that up around line 302). Two requests at once would both load the same state, both write it back, and one would be lost.

The queue, in five lines. Read the promise currently queued for this channel, or an already-finished one if there is none. Chain the new work onto it, store the result back as the new tail, and return it so the caller can await its turn. The detail that makes it reliable is .then(trabalho, trabalho): the same function is passed as both the success and the failure handler, so if the previous request threw, the next one still runs instead of the queue jamming forever.

Slack sometimes delivers the same event twice, and "ts" (the timestamp) is each message's unique id. Without this Set, a duplicate delivery would cost you a second full model run and a second answer. It lives only in memory, so restarting the bot forgets what it has seen.

app.message registers the handler: Slack calls this function for every message it sends you. The three things it hands over are the message itself, say (post into the same channel) and client (the full Slack API, used further down to edit and delete).

The first filter. Edits, deletions, joins and pinned messages all arrive as messages carrying a "subtype", and only a plain human message has none. Anything with a subtype is dropped here, which is what stops the bot answering its own edit events.
A message with no text at all is what a photo or a file upload looks like. There would be nothing to send the model, so it returns early rather than calling the brain with undefined.
The duplicate check, then recording the id, in that order. After this point the message is accepted, and the log line is your first sign of life in the terminal.

From here on, the work runs inside that channel's queue. The await means this handler waits its turn, so if you send three messages quickly, they are answered in order instead of trampling each other.

Posts the placeholder you see immediately, so you know the bot is alive while the model thinks. Keeping aviso.ts matters: that timestamp is the only way to edit or delete that exact message later. The ! tells TypeScript the value is there, since Slack types it as optional.

The real call into the brain. The channel id doubles as the conversation key, which is what gives every Slack channel its own separate memory. The third argument is the progress callback: the brain calls it whenever a tool starts, and it edits the placeholder in place rather than posting a new message. The .catch(console.log) is deliberate, and the comment above it says why: if editing the note fails, the request carries on, because the note is decoration.
The answer is logged and posted. Everything the user ever sees comes out of these two lines.

The error path. Any exception from the brain becomes a readable Slack message containing erro.message plus "send it again, I pick up where I left off". That second half is literally true: the state was saved after every step, so a retry resumes the unfinished request instead of starting over. The resuming itself happens in harness/agente.ts (around line 368).

Cleanup: the placeholder is deleted whether the request worked or failed, since this line sits after the try/catch rather than inside it. Again with .catch, because a failed cleanup must not turn a good answer into an error.

app.start() opens the socket to Slack, and nothing before this line could have received a message. Top-level await works because package.json sets "type": "module". After it prints, the process stays alive on its own, held open by the socket.

The last line starts the price watcher and hands it a way to speak: a function that posts to whichever channel it names. The watcher stores the channel with each watch, so an alert lands in the conversation that asked for it. This is the one place where output is not a reply to anything.
